title: Why doesn't pytest-cov fail with a non-zero exit code when code coverage threshold isn't met, when running on multiple directories?
text:
When the average test coverage threshold across multiple modules isn't met, pytest  doesn't  fail with a non-zero exit code, even though it should. 
 My command: 
  ❯ pytest --cov module1 --cov module2 --cov module3 --cov-report --cov-fail-under=75
  
 I get the following result: 
  FAIL Required test coverage of 75.0% not reached. Total coverage: 74.79%
  
 But the exit code remains zero: 
  ❯ echo $?
0
  
 As a result, my CI/CD pipeline passes just fine even though my coverage threshold isn't met. This causes main to have too low test coverage. 
 I've tried 
 
 Passing  --cov=module1,module2,module3  instead of having one pytest call with three different  --cov  arguments. This causes the coverage report to fail altogether, because it says that  CoverageWarning: Module module1,module2,module3 was never imported . I.e., it tries to import  module1,module2,module3  as a single module and it fails, since they are separate modules. 
 Passing the to-be-included modules in  pyproject.toml  under  [tool.coverage.run]  in the  include  argument. Problem persists: test coverage threshold failure is noted, but exit code is zero. 
 Interestingly, when you test on each of the modules individually, you do get a non-zero exit code for the module that has too low coverage. 
 On the internet, I can't really seem to find a working solution. Copilot isn't very useful here either. 
 
 Update including MWE 
 I've been able to reproduce the bug. See  this repo   README . 
 It looks like the rounding of the test coverage percentage is the issue. As e.g. in my example, the test coverage threshold isn't met (66.66% instead of the required 67%). Therefore, I rightfully see the message  FAIL Required test coverage of 67% not reached. Total coverage: 66.67% . Nonetheless, the exit code seems to look at the rounded, zero-decimal percentage values of the test coverage vs. test coverage threshold, because the exit code is zero.

  contracts, types, and usages are visible together 
 
  AI tools like GitHub Copilot, Cursor, or similar can access the  full context  of the system 
 
 
 My hypothesis is that this could improve: 
 
  refactors that touch shared APIs 
 
  propagating changes across multiple apps 
 
  consistency when updating reusable methods or types 
 
  reducing copy/paste–driven divergence 
 
 
 However, this is more an intuition than something I’ve validated extensively in production. 
  My questions are:  
 
  Have you observed real, practical benefits when using AI coding tools in a monorepo compared to multi-repo setups? 
 
  Does having the full codebase context actually improve the quality of AI suggestions/refactors?

 I checked the man page for malloc and it seems to suggest this behaviour, stating no other errors could occur: 
 
 RETURN VALUE 
 The malloc(), calloc(), realloc(), and reallocarray() functions return a pointer to the allocated memory, which is suitably aligned for any type that fits into the requested size or less.  On error, these functions return NULL and set errno.
... 
 ERRORS 
 calloc(), malloc(), realloc(), and reallocarray() can fail with the following error: 
 ENOMEM Out of memory.  Possibly, the application hit the RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA limit described in getrlimit(2).  Another reason could be that the number of mappings created by the caller process exceeded the limit specified by /proc/sys/vm/max_map_count. 
 
  and also, ChatGPT says so too...  
But I decided that it's better to be safe than sorry. 
 The reason I'm doing this is that I'm creating my own web server for fun, and it would be a lot easier to send  507 Insufficient Memory  whenever malloc fails instead of having 2 cases every time I write malloc in my code.

I'm experimenting with a documentation architecture aimed at improving how AI coding agents (specifically Cursor agents) understand and navigate a project. 
 The goal is to reduce the amount of code the agent needs to inspect by giving it structured, hierarchical context about the project. 
 Current approach

   agents.md  defines the global rules and conventions. 
 
  Each lower-level  .md  acts as an  index for the components below it . 
 
  The structure "capillarizes" down to folder-level documentation. 
 
 
 In  agents.md  I also define how the other  .md  files should be structured. 
 Structure of each module  .md  
 Each documentation file defines two main things: 
  Skill

  Spec

  what dependencies it has 
 
 
 The goal is that the agent can quickly identify which components are relevant without scanning unnecessary parts of the codebase. 
 Update rule

text:
I’m designing a high-volume analytics system and I’m trying to choose the data model before the dataset becomes too large to change easily. 
 Current setup: 
 
  Custom app events are stored in ClickHouse 
 
  Device and user records are stored in MongoDB 
 
  MongoDB is where current device/user dimensions live, such as: 
 
  os_name 
 
  os_version 
 
  device_model 
 
  app_version 
 
  current user_uuid 
 
 
 
  ClickHouse is the event store 
 
 
 Important concepts: 
 
  device_uuid 
 
  user_uuid 
 
  client event timestamp 
 
  server-side received_at 
 
 
 Important product behavior: 
 
  A device can start as anonymous 
 For example, at first  user_uuid = device_uuid  
 
  Later the same device can become a real user 
 For example,  user_uuid = John  
 
  When that happens, past anonymous events should also be attributed to the real user 
 
 
 Because of that, storing user_uuid directly in the huge ClickHouse events table creates expensive update/mutation problems. 
 So one design I’m considering is: 
 events table in ClickHouse, immutable: 
  project_id 
device_uuid 
timestamp 
received_at 
event_code 
session_id 
properties
  
 Separate ownership table in ClickHouse: 
  project_id 
device_uuid 
valid_from 
valid_to 
user_uuid
  
 Then user resolution is done by joining events to ownership intervals using device_uuid + received_at. 
 Short example: 
 
  10:00 device D1 is anonymous, so owner is D1 
 
  10:05 and 10:06 events are inserted for device D1 
 
  10:10 user logs in, now owner becomes John 
 
  Those past anonymous events should also appear under John 
 
 
 My concern is not ingestion. My concern is analytics later. 
 For example, I may need queries like: 
 
  unique users who did app_open -> permission_granted 
 
  windowFunnel by user 
 
  retention / cohort analysis by user 
 
  “show events from iOS 18.6 devices for users who later converted” 
 
  segment by event properties + resolved user + device/app dimensions

Exclusive Load/Store instructions fail with some MMU configurations on real hardware (Cortex-A53)
text:
I run into a strange issue (can't explain it myself) when using the exclusive load ( ldaxr ,  ldxr , ...) and store ( stxr , ...) instructions on real hardware (Raspberry Pi 3B+ -> Cortex A-53). These instructions working properly in a QEMU emulation, but  failing  on real hardware when the  caches  are  disabled . 
 The exclusive load and store instructions are required in locking mechanism (like  Spinloop  and  Mutex  implementations for bare-metal environments). They work only if I enable caches (instruction and data) on real hardware. If the caches are not enabled, these instructions fails and cause a infinite loop (dead lock) in code. 
 Can somebody explain this behavior? I also searched in the  architecture reference manual , but didn't find any hint currently. 
 (This is a follow-up question from my  answer  for this  SO question .) 
  UPDATE:  
 I must admit took a conversation with ChatGPT now. ChatGPT helped me and gave me a plausible answer. Unfortunately because of the SO policy I can't provide ChatGPT's answer. But in my original question there were lacking some information. 
 The MMU is enabled in my bare-metal environment. The mutex/spinlock is implemented in  Rust  using atomic operations, which the compiler compiles to AArch64 exclusive load and store instructions ( LDXR / STXR ,  LDAXR / STLXR ). On the Raspberry Pi 3B+ (Cortex-A53), the atomic operations work correctly when the shared RAM is mapped as cacheable Normal memory and the Data Cache is enabled. When the RAM is mapped as non-cacheable or the Data Cache is disabled,  STXR  repeatedly fails and the lock enters an infinite retry loop. The same code works under QEMU. 
 Hope this helps other users facing the same issue too.

title: Why does my lyrics lookup return no results for songs that exist in the database?
text:
I'm using claude to work on an app that allow to find lyrics for the current song playing (real time running sync if LYCLIB already have synced file, auto-sync if it's not); I currently have 3 problems and unfortunately neither claude or chatgpt can give me a good recommendation. 
 
  lyrics finder : How I do is clean up title -> check saved copy from local (for auto-sync only) -> ask LYCLIB to pull the lyrics -> ask VocalDB if LYCLIB don't have it -> check out YT music panel if can't find anything from 2 previous DB -> show the lyrics (either sync or non-sync) 
* The problem is it takes forever, even with clean up, the program doesn't show lyrics for songs that had a version in LYCLIB (or VocalDB) and return as 0, how can I optimize the time of searching for lyrics, and fix this false negative return? 
 
 What I have tried: 
 
 LRCLIB endpoint order: /api/get-cached → /api/search (by fields) → /api/search?q= → /api/get last, because /api/get is slow and sometimes answers 503. Result: fewer slow calls, but a lookup is still several requests in a row. 
 Overload handling: LRCLIB answered “503 ServerOverloaded” to about 1 request in 4 on bad days. Each request now gets 2 retries (after 1 s, then 2 s), with a 10 s timeout. A failed lookup is retried after 10 s, 30 s, then every minute. A 429 (rate limit) pauses all lookups for the time LRCLIB asks, default 60 s, up to 15 min. Result: fewer outright failures, but it’s the main reason a lookup can “take forever”. 
 Title cleanup: split Project SEKAI’s “Song / Singers” titles into title and artists; strip [VOCALOID ver.] and a trailing “MV”; map units YouTube Music writes in English to LRCLIB’s Japanese names. Result: fixed Teratera and others. 
 VocaDB alternate names: romaji and English titles get looked up again on LRCLIB under VocaDB’s Japanese names. Result: 16 of 37 songs that only VocaDB had then got timed lyrics from LRCLIB. 
 Cache: “not found” is saved for 3 days, a VocaDB answer for 7 days, keye
